Cheap, concurrency-safe clone.

  • You must call clone.set_dataset(ds) in each worker before using compare_vectors or score_dataset.

class gal.oracles.oracles.SurpriseOracle(prior_type: str = 'independent', *, phi: Callable[[float, float], float] | None = None, name: str | None = None, **prior_kwargs)[source]¶

Bases: Oracle

Parameters:

  • prior_type (str) – Key registered in priors.PRIOR_FACTORY.

  • phi (callable(fo, fe) -> float, optional) – Surprise function. Default: lambda fo, fe: log(fo) - log(fe).

  • name (str, optional) – Identifier used in logs / result tables.

  • **prior_kwargs – Extra arguments forwarded to the prior constructor.

class gal.oracles.oracles.MDLOracle(c0: float = 8.0, c_item: float = 4.0, name: str | None = None)[source]¶

Bases: Oracle

MDL-based interestingness: positive values mean the rule compresses the data better than chance.

Expected columns in dataset.df:

support     -- support of the union (|X ∪ Y|)
supportX    -- support of the antecedent (|X|)
supportY    -- support of the consequent (|Y|, single item assumed)
len_X       -- number of items in the antecedent
len_Y       -- number of items in the consequent

class gal.oracles.priors.BayesianNetworkPrior(max_parents: int = 2, device: str = 'cuda', batch_size: int = 1000000)[source]¶

Bases: object

Sparse Bayesian network learned with pgmpy, but evaluated on the GPU with PyTorch. Assumes binary (0/1) item variables.

Parameters:

  • max_parents (int (≤ 2 keeps CPTs tiny, default 2))

  • device ("cuda"|"cpu")

  • batch_size (int rules per GPU chunk in expected_batch)

fit(transactions: pandas.DataFrame, *, max_iter: int = 300, epsilon: float = 0.001, structure_sample: int | None = 10000, use_chow_liu_start: bool = True, show_progress: bool = True)[source]¶

Learn a sparse Bayesian network from binary transactions.

Fast-path tricks used in this implementation:

  • Row subsampling (structure_sample) – limit the number of rows considered during the structure search; CPDs are still fitted on the full dataset.

  • Good starting point (use_chow_liu_start) – initialise the hill-climbing search with a Chow–Liu tree instead of an empty graph.

  • Early convergence (max_iter and epsilon) – stop the optimisation when improvements become negligible.

Parameters are exposed so callers can trade speed against accuracy.

expected(rule: Dict[str, object]) → float[source]¶
expected_batch(dataset) → ndarray[source]¶

Bases: Prior

Fast approximation of a Bayesian network: optimal tree structure learned with the Chow-Liu algorithm, CPDs fitted with Bayesian estimation, and stored as GPU tensors for batched scoring.
